Absolutely not! Never ever! A short story and a long story. I consider myself very kind and love helping people. Giving my umbrella to someone at the bus stop when it is raining if I am driving (if I offer a ride, they think I'm a serial killer), helping someone on the interstate with gas, jump, even offering to carry groceries if some purchased more than they can carry and have to stop every 50 feet to rest.

Short story: I was on the bus and it broke down at a giant intersection, tons of cars. A man hobbles to the front of traffic, hobbles through the center lane with his cup, unshaven, holding a sign, I couldn't read it from my location. 10 people gave some money. I saw change and also bills. When the light turned green, he straightened his stride and walked with full strength to the bus stop and sat there, a reached under the seat where there was a 24-pack of bottled water. He grabbed one and took a drink and waited for the next red light and did the same thing two more times before my bus took off. I was so upset! i couldn't believe he didn't even wait for the kind people to drive off before showing what a con he was. Yes, this was the short story.

Long story: I tell this true story to young homeless people when they try to chat me up for cash.

When I was 15, I ran away from home. I confided in someone about my sexuality and word got out and I was not treated well. So I left. After about a week on the street and brainstorming I can across a solution. This is what I did. There are areas in all cities that are safe and full of families and professionals. They recycle. I would never DARE show my face on the street if I was dirty, unshaven, stinky, etc. So I stayed in the alleys. I saw the recycling bins full of plastic and aluminum. I found some large plastic bags with handles like you see some homeless people with on the train with, etc. I would sleep in the alley next to some garages and when I would wake from the sound of people going to work, the busses, etc I would start my journey of collecting cans. I made sure to keep the dumpsters cleaning remember where I started and ended when my two bags were full. I would walk about 2-3 miles to the nearest recycling center and I would wait in line with other homeless people with shopping carts and bags as well. I would get about $4-5 for my two huge bags of crushed cans. I would return to the alley where I left off and continued this until nightfall. At the end of the day, I would end up with $15-$20. I would go to a $5 barber, I would go to a laundrymat and wash clothes, since I only owned about two sets of clothing. I would change at McDonald's and shave in the bathroom. I would shower once a week at a YMCA after paying a $5 one day entry. Everything I owned was in a backpack. Then I would go to a major street and go door to door asking for work. That is how I got my first job at McDonald's coincidentally. I worked during the day and still collected cans at night. I opened a bank account with my first check, still wash up at the McDonald's where I worked and continued my $5 haircuts. After two months I was able to get a studio. I didn't smoke, I didn't drink, I did;t do drugs, I didn't steal, I didn't ask for money on the street. I remember seeing some homeless people with shoppings carts so full of metal and I wondered what they did with off of their money.

So when I see a physically and mentally capable person asking for money, I just can't see myself giving it up when they appear to not really trying. I suspect that people only give money when they are elsewhere. If there was a homeless drunk or drug addict outside their home or apartment building that they saw everyday, they wouldn't be as generous. As an adult and business owner I can't stand to see people give handouts, that just keeps them in the areas continuing to ask.

I hope I made my point of view clear. Thanks for reading. :-)

Depends, if I'm in my car absolutely not--that would be reinforcing the dangerous behavior of approaching moving vehicles to get money. If I'm walking however, and I'm not in any sort of hurry I will ask what they are going to use the money for. If they say something like "food" I will ask what food and offer to buy it for them. Usually they will just walk away angrily. If they are honest and say booze or drugs, I'll give them a bit of change if I have it available if for nothing else than a reward for honesty. I have had a few take me up on the food offer though and I end up picking them up something inexpensive that they want. to eat. Of course if I get any sort of feeling they are con artists I tell them politely to fuck off. It's not hard to tell the difference between those people and the people who are really down and out.

Yes, I do, and I'm not judgmental enough to say that they'll waste it, or that they don't deserve to have it. It's a few bucks. I give it to them and be on my way. How can I act like I know what their life has been like? A lot of people seem to believe they have them all figured out. Shit happens. You don't have to be mean because someone has fallen under hard times, and you think they did something bad to get that way. Sometimes self-responsibility and doing the right thing doesn't work out.

For example, what if you went bankrupt trying to pay for your wife's medical bills? Then she died, and all your assets were seized? I mean, really, there are a lot of situations. Not everyone is a stupid drug addict that self-inflicted their wounds.
Never. Most are living a better life than the donors. I lived in a building central to a city center and 2/3 of the beggars lived there. They were nice apartments that didn't come cheap.

I often do but I have conditions.

If I have loose change in my pocket when a typical panhandler asks for something then I will give at least a little something, even if I suspect they want booze or cigarettes-- it's very rare to see folks like this completely rummy and falling down drunk plus besides, I generally think the spirit of giving to someone who needs a hand should be promoted.

That said, I never give to panhandlers walking up to stopped cars, and both panhandlers that tell a bunch of lies or start expecting a handout every time they see me are all big turnoffs. If they tell me some convoluted story about how they need to get home and then I see them again, especially if they try telling me that same and now outdated story, they're effectively shitlisted.

It's a case by case thing. I've been homeless and destitute. I put myself together and now live a pretty damn good life, but I'll never forget the days when a $10 windfall could make my week. I tried panhandling once or twice, when i was really hard up but i couldn't get over the sense of humiliation.

Generally, I don't give to the young and able bodied. Not because I judge them, but because I don't want to reinforce or reward begging when they have so many other options.

When someone asks me for some change, I'm often coming out of the store having dropped $150 on scotch or even $30 on a movie or similar. It's really hard to justify why I can't share a small part of my fortune with them. Yes I earned what I have, but it doesn't mean I've forgotten what a little can mean some days.

Sometimes I like to go above and beyond. Not too often, but every once in a while you'll see in someone's eyes that they are well and truely broken. Lost faith in others, humanity, themselves. Something kicked them hard. Those I sit down with and have a chat. Talk and listen and if I think it will help give them more than pocket change. $20, $50, once $100. It's only partly about the money. When you're down and out the sense of being alone is the most crippling part. Someone taking the time to listen and giving something freely can carry them for a week or a month. Who knows, it might tip a scale somewhere that helps them get out of whatever they're stuck in.

Fundamentally, it's about humanity. I don't care what they do with the money. Smokes, booze or a haircut and clothes for a job - not my call. I can't fix them and won't pretend that I can. What I can do is share a little humanity and acknowledge that they too matter. Doesn't matter if it's $0.35 or $100.
